findings.title: restart_review re-enters the review on every supervisor step, not once: review_restarted never survives single_step
findings.description: `review_restarted` is a local variable in drive(). In production, drive only runs through `automatic-step`, which uses single_step=True: after one invoke it returns None and the step exits 75, whether the invoke succeeded or failed. The next step is a new process with review_restarted=False. restart_review still returns True, because no combined status and no review-worktree exist, so the review is re-entered again. The guard only works in the test, which calls drive() without single_step (test_repair.py ReviewFailedBeforeALaunch). RUNBOOK:284 ('re-enters a review that launched no reviewer once ... and stops if the same failure comes back') and the commit message are false under the real supervisor.
findings.failure_scenario: I confirmed this with a probe in the scratchpad (r4probe/probe_restart_review.py): the ReviewFailedBeforeALaunch setup with git_worktree failing on every review-worktree attempt, and drive(single_step=True) called 8 times. All 8 returned None (exit 75), with 8 worktree attempts and 7 'Re-entering the review' events. Under supervise() this repeats until the 45-step budget is used up. Each repeat runs git_worktree's lock-retry backoff. The run then ends with 'Automatic controller restart limit exhausted' instead of the classified 'Non-retryable graph failure' carrying Git's error.
findings.suggested_fix: Persist the one-shot guard. For example, write `review-restarted.json` with the error before re-entering, and have restart_review return False when it exists (it can be removed once automatic-review.json exists). Alternatively, count the 'Re-entering the review' events. Change the test to drive with single_step=True so the supervisor's pattern is covered.

findings.title: A TransientInfraError from a review node that already recorded a terminal state exits 69/75 as resumable, but resume is 'Non-retryable'
findings.description:
Round 3 raises every TransientInfraError from graph.invoke, so the step exits 69 and `automatic` exits 75, and it logs UNAVAILABLE_NOTE ('Nothing was stopped: the native sessions keep running ... resume with automatic --live'). It does this even when the node turned the outage into a terminal state first:
(a) `_review_print`: popen_claude raises TransientInfraError after its 60 s grace. The except BaseException at 884-893 terminates the print jobs already running and sets the combined status to `blocked`.
(b) `rebind_reviewers` (602-607): reconcile_reviewer's inventory raises TransientInfraError on the resume that RUNBOOK:247 promises rebinds a reviewer interrupted during its settle. The status is marked `needs_reconciliation`.
On the next `automatic --live`, neither resume_interrupted_review nor restart_review matches, and drive raises 'Non-retryable graph failure'. Before round 3 these paths ended with exit 1 (blocked). Now `automatic`/`launch --automatic`/`resume` exit 75, and the note claims nothing was stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: I confirmed case (a) with a probe (r4probe/probe_print_outage.py): print transport, two reviewers, and the second popen_claude raising TransientInfraError. drive(single_step=True) raised TransientInfraError (step exit 69), the combined status was `blocked`, and the last event was 'controller interrupted ... Nothing was stopped: the native sessions keep running ... resume'. The next drive raised 'Non-retryable graph failure; inspect retained evidence'.
findings.suggested_fix: In drive's TransientInfraError branch, raise (exit 69) only when the failed state is resumable: freeze_failure(failed) or review_interrupted(runtime, failed). Otherwise fall through to the normal classification so the run ends blocked. In addition, rebind_reviewers should re-raise TransientInfraError after setting combined['interrupted'] instead of marking needs_reconciliation, and _review_print should not claim 'nothing was stopped'.

findings.title: A `claude stop` that exited non-zero stays `issued: true`, so a retry in a respawn gap records `stopped: true` without stopping
findings.description: stop_session records `issued=True` before `claude stop` runs, and resets it only when run_claude raises TransientInfraError. A stop that ran and exited non-zero keeps `issued: true`. That is what the finding-10 verifier and the docstring of test_a_stop_follows_a_session_an_update_respawned_under_a_new_pid describe for a background service that is restarting. On the retry (resume after REVIEW_STOP_NOTE, or stop_workers after a blocked wait), a listing that omits the session skips the `matching or issued is False` branch. The old PID, which the respawn ended, is dead, so `stopped: true` is saved with no `claude stop` issued. RUNBOOK:289 says only a stop already issued counts a missing session as stopped; a failed stop counts here.
findings.failure_scenario: I confirmed this with a probe (r4probe/probe_failed_stop_gap.py). Attempt 1 listed a live row, `claude stop` returned 1, and the error was 'Stop failed for ui' with intent `{issued: True, stopped: False}`. On the retry the listings were `[]`, `[]` and the recorded PID was dead. The retry made 0 `claude stop` calls and saved `{stopped: True, issued: True}`, while the respawned session comes back under a new PID. After that, stop_workers either fails permanently with 'A stopped worker was restarted', or passes while the row is missing, and attach-one reports the session as stopped by the controller.
findings.suggested_fix: When `claude stop` exits non-zero, save `issued: False` before raising. The next attempt then looks through a gap with stop_row and issues the stop again. Alternatively, record `stopped` for an issued stop only after a listing shows the id's row terminal (for example `claude agents --json --all`), not after a single empty listing and a dead old PID.

findings.title: wait_reviews pre-pass re-reads the live completion file at any session state, so a restart can block or flip an accepted verdict
findings.description: A verdict accepted before a restart is not persisted: only `accepted_at` is saved (the accept() helper). The new pre-pass calls read_review_completion on the current `<node>.completion.json` without listing the session. Before round 3, a restarted controller read the file only once the reviewer was idle or done. Now the file is read while the reviewer may still be working on a follow-up typed in its pane, which RUNBOOK:246 names as expected. A half-written file raises 'Malformed review completion signal', which blocks the reviewer and, through _accept_native, stops every reviewer. A rewritten file changes the verdict that a controller which never restarted would have kept in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: Two reviewers. A approves and is accepted (accepted_at saved), and B is still working. The operator types a follow-up in A's pane, and A starts rewriting its completion file. An update then makes the controller exit 75, and the operator resumes. rebind_reviewers runs, then wait_reviews, and the pre-pass reads A's partial file. accept() raises, A is marked `blocked`, and _accept_native blocks the whole review and stops both reviewers. Without the restart, the run would have used A's approval.
findings.suggested_fix: At acceptance, persist the decision (or the completion file's sha256) in the reviewer's status. In the pre-pass, reuse the persisted decision, or verify the digest and fall back to the idle/done read in the loop.

findings.title: stop_workers aborts at the first lane whose stop raises, so a blocked run with a terminal or changed-identity lane leaves later lanes running
findings.description:
stop_workers calls stop_session for each lane with no per-lane handling. Round 3 routes stop_session through stop_row/UpdateGaps, which raises for:
- a `stopped`/`failed` row (verified_row's terminal check),
- any identity refusal,
- a gap longer than 30 s (TransientInfraError).
So the lane whose condition blocked the wait also makes stop_workers raise at that lane. drive records only 'Could not confirm worker stop', and every lane after it in the order keeps running. RUNBOOK:34 and RUNBOOK:289, rewritten in round 3, say 'a `stopped` or `failed` session or a changed session identity still stops the sessions'. stop_reviewers already continues past failures.
findings.failure_scenario: Lanes ui and adapter, in that order. ui's row comes back under a changed identity (for example 'Native Claude UUID changed'), so wait_handoffs raises a RuntimeError. drive records `controller blocked` and calls stop_workers, and stop_session('ui') raises the same identity refusal from stop_row. adapter's live session is never stopped and keeps using quota after the run is blocked.
findings.suggested_fix: Make stop_workers try every lane, collect the failures and raise one combined error afterwards, as stop_reviewers does. Optionally, have stop_session record `stopped: true` for a terminal row of the intent's own background id.

findings.title: Reviewer pre-pass stops at the first blocking verdict and drops verdicts accepted later in declared order from review.json
findings.description: The pre-pass for verdicts accepted before a restart goes through `state.ids` in declared order and returns as soon as one accepted decision blocks (`if accepted and ... and decision_blocks(accept(...)): return decisions`). Reviewers declared after that one also have `accepted_at`, but they are never put back into `decisions`. `combined_review` then writes them with `verdict: null, accepted_at: null`, and their findings are left out of the union. A controller that never stopped would have recorded both verdicts, because `wait_reviews` returned {coverage, general}. The code comment says the pre-pass exists so an accepted verdict is not dropped from the combined result, and RUNBOOK:244-245 says accepted verdicts are retained in review.json.
findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed with a probe on the TwoReviewerCompletionTests fixture (reviewers general, coverage). coverage writes approved with a P2 finding and is accepted at t=100 while general works. general then writes blocked and is accepted, so wait_reviews returns {coverage: approved, general: blocked}. check_independence next hits an update respawn gap longer than 30 s, which raises TransientInfraError, records the review's `interrupted` marker, and makes `automatic` exit 75. On `automatic --live`, the pre-pass reads general first, sees the block and returns {general: blocked}. combined_review then gives [(general, blocked), (coverage, None, None)] with 1 finding instead of 2. coverage's status file still says `accepted`, which contradicts review.json. This is the exact update-respawn path round 3 targets.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore every accepted reviewer before deciding. First loop: `for rid in state.ids: if state.statuses[rid].get('accepted_at') and rid not in decisions: accept(rid, state.statuses[rid]['accepted_at'])`. Then `if any(decision_blocks(d) for d in decisions.values()): return decisions`. Add a two-reviewer test where the first-declared reviewer blocks after the second approved, followed by a restart, and assert that review.json keeps both verdicts and all findings.

findings.title: Pre-pass re-reads a mutable completion file: after a restart an accepted verdict can change (blocked becomes approved) and keep its old accepted_at
findings.description: accept() persists only `status: accepted` and `accepted_at`, not the decision it accepted. On a restart the pre-pass calls read_review_completion again on the reviewer's current file, whatever its session state (RUNBOOK:245 anticipates a follow-up typed in its pane). The reviewer session keeps running after acceptance until stop_reviewers, and it can rewrite its file; the launch token, bundle and candidate are unchanged, so the rewritten file validates. A restarted controller therefore decides on content that was never accepted, and review.json pairs it with the original accepted_at. A controller that never stopped would have kept the first decision. The pre-pass also reads the file while the session may be `working`, so a read that races a rewrite gets a malformed file and blocks the review and stops every reviewer.
findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed with a probe on TwoReviewerCompletionTests. general writes verdict blocked and is accepted at t=100; wait_reviews returns {general: blocked} and the status is persisted as accepted. Before _decide, check_independence raises TransientInfraError (exit 75). The operator argues with general in its pane, and general rewrites its file as approved. On `automatic --live`, the pre-pass reads approved and does not return. The loop accepts coverage, and the resumed wait_reviews returns {general: approved, coverage: approved}. _decide approves and the run integrates a candidate whose accepted verdict was blocked. review.json shows general approved with the accepted_at of the blocked acceptance.
findings.suggested_fix: In accept(), persist what was accepted: `status.update(status='accepted', accepted_at=..., decision=decision, completion_sha256=digest_file(path))`. In the pre-pass, restore `decisions[rid] = status['decision']` without re-deciding from the file, or re-validate the binding and refuse (block, with a clear error) when the file's digest differs from `completion_sha256`. Add a test that rewrites an accepted reviewer's file before a restart.

findings.title: A rerun after a failed Enter presses Enter without checking the input still holds the text, then marks the answer delivered
findings.description: After send-text succeeds, `typed: true` is recorded. When Enter then fails, every later herdr rerun only runs `send-keys Enter`, as long as process-info shows `claude attach <id>`, and answer_main then sets `delivered: true`. Nothing checks that the session's input still holds the text. RUNBOOK:289 documents that an update respawns idle sessions, explicitly including a lane paused on a question, under a new PID. A new process does not carry the old one's unsubmitted input, so after a respawn the rerun submits an empty input. The answer is then recorded as delivered, and every later `answer` is refused ("no unanswered question"). RUNBOOK:56 and the failure message claim that after a failed Enter the text is already in the session's input.
findings.failure_scenario: `answer RUN ui "Use option B"`: process-info shows attach-one plus `claude attach bg-ui`, send-text succeeds (typed: true), and send-keys Enter times out (herdr's 15 s timeout), so the command exits 1 saying the rerun presses Enter only. Before the operator reruns, a Claude Code update restarts the service and respawns the idle ui session under a new PID, and attach-one reattaches. The rerun passes pane_attachment, presses Enter on an empty prompt, and marks delivered: true. ui never received the answer and stays idle. Its deadline, which has run since the answer was recorded, expires, and drive blocks the run and stops every worker.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the session's live PID from `claude agents --json` (InteractiveSessions.locate) with the `typed` step. On a typed rerun, press Enter only while that PID is unchanged. Otherwise do not submit blindly: retype the text, or refuse with "look at pane <pane>: press Enter if its input holds the text, else rerun with --no-herdr" and leave `delivered` false. Add an AnswerDelivery test where the session PID changes between the failed Enter and the rerun.

result.reasoning:
I could not refute it; the finding holds at 74fdc9e.

- **The guard is a local variable.** `review_restarted` is set at workflow/automatic.py:1210 and only lives inside one drive() call.

After one `graph.invoke`, drive() returns None at automatic.py:1292-1293, whether the invoke succeeded or failed. A non-transient failure goes to `settle_interruption` and then to `return None`. The step exits 75, and supervise() (automatic.py:1077-1089) starts a new process for the next step, where `review_restarted` is False again.
- **restart_review never turns itself off.** It checks only three things: `review` is the failed node, `automatic-review.json` (the combined status) is missing, and `review-worktree/` is missing (automatic.py:1142-1155). None of those change when `git worktree add` fails (Git leaves no directory behind) or when `validate_bundle` raises before the worktree is created. So every new step re-enters the review.
- **The probe confirms it.** I ran the probe (scratchpad/r4probe/probe_restart_review.py) from /home/agentops/dev/mdm-integrate: drive(single_step=True) called 8 times returned [None]*8, with 8 review-worktree attempts and 7 "Re-entering the review" events.
- **Effect under the real supervisor.**

  - A lock-contention failure also pays git_worktree's backoff of 5 attempts, about 3.75 s, on every step.

- **Docs and test don't match.** RUNBOOK.md:284 ("re-enters a review that launched no reviewer once ... and stops if the same failure comes back"), the restart_review docstring and the commit message are false for the real `automatic --live` path.

Make the one-shot guard survive across step processes but reset for each `automatic --live` run, so that a new supervisor started after the operator fixes the cause still gets one re-entry, as the test at test_repair.py:688 expects.

4. Add a test that runs the ReviewFailedBeforeALaunch setup with drive(runtime, single_step=True) in a loop, or runs supervise() with the steps mocked. Assert exactly one "Re-entering the review" event, and that the second step raises "Non-retryable graph failure" with Git's error.

result.reasoning:
I could not refute the mechanism. At 74fdc9e the defect is real, but P1 overstates it; P2 fits better.

Code, verified:
- The guard `review_restarted` is a plain local set in drive() (workflow/automatic.py:1210 and 1263-1265). Nothing persists it.
- The only production caller of drive() is `automatic-step` (workflow/pipeline.py:973), which calls it with single_step=True. supervise() (workflow/automatic.py:1075-1090) runs each step as a new `python -m workflow automatic-step` subprocess, up to 45 of them.
- After a non-transient review failure, the except branch neither raises nor persists anything (automatic.py:1269-1289). `finally` reports, then `if single_step: return None` (1292), so the step exits 75.
- In the next process, review_restarted is False again. restart_review() still returns True, because a failed git_worktree (automatic.py:576) leaves neither combined status nor review-worktree/.

Probe: I wrote my own under scratchpad/sk2/probe_sk2.py. It uses the RepairFixture, makes git_worktree fail every time for review-worktree, and calls drive(single_step=True) 5 times. Result: `[None, None, None, None, None]`, 5 worktree attempts, 4 'Re-entering the review' events, and no review-worktree or combined status. So every step exits 75 and re-enters again.

The only test, ReviewFailedBeforeALaunch (test_repair.py:658), calls drive(self.runtime) without single_step. It checks an in-process loop that production never uses.

These claims are false under the real supervisor:
- RUNBOOK.md:284 ("re-enters a review that launched no reviewer once ... and stops if the same failure comes back")
- the inline comment at automatic.py:1265 ("the same failure again stops it")
- the commit message

Why P2, not P1:
- The repetition is bounded by supervise's 45 steps.
- The review failed before any launch, and each status is saved before its launch, so no reviewer session is launched or launched twice and no verdict is touched.
- The workers are already frozen.
- Both outcomes exit 1 from `automatic`. The old path went step exit 1 to 'Automatic controller blocked (exit 1)'. The new path ends in 'Automatic controller restart limit exhausted' with no classified message.
- The real costs:
  - about 44 extra controller processes, each running git_worktree's lock retries (5 attempts, 0.25s doubling backoff, about 3.75s each), so a few minutes;
  - a flood of identical timeline events;
  - a final message that no longer says it was a non-retryable review failure.
- The same repeat applies to any other deterministic review failure that happens before the worktree exists, such as validate_bundle or validate_automatic raising. Each would be retried about 44 times instead of stopping at once.

It is a real guarantee/doc mismatch with a weak test, but the run is not silently wrong and no invariant about sessions or verdicts breaks.
result.suggested_fix:
Persist the one-shot guard in the run directory so it survives the automatic-step process boundary:
- In drive(), before re-entering, save `review-restarted.json` holding the review error (for example `save_json(runtime.directory / "review-restarted.json", {"error": error})`).
- Have restart_review() return False when that file exists.
- Clear the marker once combined status (automatic-review.json) exists, or in settle_interruption after a successful review invoke. A later `automatic --live` by the operator, for example after deleting a stale .lock, should re-enter once more, as the RUNBOOK promises. So also clear the marker when supervise() starts, or record the supervisor PID/start in it and compare.
- Drop the local `review_restarted` variable.
- Change ReviewFailedBeforeALaunch to loop drive(self.runtime, single_step=True) until it raises, as supervise does. It should assert two worktree attempts, one re-entry and a 'Non-retryable' stop.
- Keep RUNBOOK.md:284 as written once the code matches it.

label: verify:outage-and-drive:stop_workers aborts at the first lane wh#1

result.reasoning:
This is not a defect at 74fdc9e. The behaviour is intended, documented and tested, and the half-written-file race cannot happen in practice.

1. The design is deliberate and the docs match the code. workflow/RUNBOOK.md, in the Deadline bullet of section "Automatic mode: the review step", says: "A reviewer whose file was accepted before the controller stopped (`accepted_at` in its status) is read again whatever its session does now (a follow-up typed in its pane) ... a file that no longer validates blocks as on its first read." The pre-pass in workflow/automatic.py:517-522 does exactly that. The test workflow/test_automatic.py:706-744 (test_a_verdict_accepted_before_a_restart_stays_accepted_while_its_session_works_again) checks both parts: the pre-pass reads the file while the session is working or blocked, and a re-read file that is rejected (stale bundle_sha256) blocks and records the error. So blocking on a file that no longer validates is the specified behaviour, not an accident.

2. A half-written completion file cannot be seen. The reviewer can only write through Claude Code's Write/Edit tools; its tools are Read, Glob, Grep and Write, and it has no Bash. The installed claude binary writes files atomically: it writes a `.tmp.<pid>.<hex>` file with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, fsyncs it, then renames it over the target. It only falls back to writing in place when the rename fails with a filesystem error, which does not apply to the run directory. So read_review_completion sees either the old complete file or the new complete one, never a partial one. The step "accept() raises 'Malformed review completion signal'" does not happen.

3. The "flipped verdict" part is not new in round 3 and is not silently wrong. Before round 3, a restarted controller also started with an empty state.decisions, because ReviewStatus.__init__ does not persist decisions. It re-read the same reviewer's completion file once the session was idle or done, so it would also have picked up a rewritten file. Round 3 only changed the read to happen whatever the session's state; it did not start the re-read. The re-read file must still match this run's run_id, node_id, launch_token, bundle_sha256 and candidate_commit. A rewrite would therefore be the reviewer's own later verdict, which the protocol forbids it to write ("do not modify it afterwards"). The run is not being fed foreign data. The difference from a controller that never restarted is a documented design choice, not a broken guarantee.

The scenario would need all of these together: an operator follow-up, a reviewer that breaks its protocol, and a controller restart during a write that is atomic anyway. The only harm that remains is the documented fail-closed block, so nothing here reaches P2.
result.suggested_fix: No fix is needed. As an optional hardening for consistency, acceptance could save the file's sha256 in the reviewer's status. The pre-pass would then use the saved decision when the digest still matches, and otherwise fall back to the idle/done read in the loop.

**When it happens.** The first controller must have accepted both verdicts. That means `wait_reviews` returned, because an accepted block returns at once. Then something between that return and `_decide` has to cut the controller short:
- `check_independence` (lines 746-760) raises `TransientInfraError`, either from `inventory()` or from an UpdateGaps gap that outlasts the grace; or
- a Ctrl-C arrives.
In both cases `combined.status` stays `running`. `review_candidate` then runs `rebind_reviewers` and `_accept_native`, and the pre-pass is reached.

Code (workflow/guardrails.py:898-905): `herdr pane send-text` runs through `herdr()` (workflow/herdr.py), which calls `subprocess.run(..., timeout=15)`. If Herdr takes longer than 15 seconds, subprocess.run kills the CLI child and raises `TimeoutExpired`. `deliver_answer` turns that into a RuntimeError before `mark_delivered(..., "typed")` runs, so `typed` is never recorded and `delivered` stays false. On the next `answer`, `undelivered_answer` returns the same entry, and `deliver_answer` skips the Enter-only branch because `typed` is not set. It calls send-text again. The timeout does not tell us whether Herdr already typed the text, and the code's own error message admits this ("it may be in pane {pane}'s input already: look before rerunning answer"). So in this case a rerun can type the answer a second time.

The repository's test confirms this: `test_a_rerun_after_a_failed_send_text_types_the_answer_and_a_timeout_says_to_look_first` (workflow/test_guardrails.py:1665-1681) asserts that the rerun after the TimeoutExpired calls `["process-info", "send-text", "send-keys"]`.
